Axiom MTS here. What you describe is pretty close to how we formalised this proof, which is scattered across more than 500 articles and books: a swarm of agents was tasked with going through all these sources.

One challenge is assembling everything into a coherent whole, since the same informal concept can be formalised in slightly different but incompatible ways.

As someone with a highly uneven and kinda basic maths background, I'd have thought that simplification of a proof, and pulling things into a coherent whole would be exactly what computers excel at, but everything I've seen (or heard) suggests that's not really the case. Are you able to explain why?

There are some (typically small) simplifications that computers are indeed good at. These could be thought of as analogous to compiler optimizations - they’ll see that your proof is basically composing several lemmas and that some of the work in the middle can be removed so it can just do that. In many cases with lean if you post a short to medium-length proof into an llm it can suggest these types of small improvements for you.

What they’re not that great at is the type of improvements that really make a big difference: big simplifications etc. This is not super suprising when you understand how this works.

Firstly proofs in lean (and I think many other assistants) are essentially functions which take hypotheses and instantiate a particular type. That type being equivalent (due to the Curry-Howard correspondence) to a proof of some proposition. The assistant uses dependent type theory to make sure all the types match up at each step, which is what makes it rigorous. So the task of simplifying a proof is basically finding a route through an infinite-dimensional space where you know your starting location and the desired end point, but at any step you can go in basically any direction you like so long as you can justify your step. You justify a step by either choosing from a (vast at this point) library of lemmas and theorems that are in your standard library, or by recursively building the proof/function you need to justify the step you want to take using this same process you’re trying to use for simplification. This is incredibly flexible, but means you’re actually spoiled for choice and planning is hard.

Secondly, in “pen and paper” proofs, LLMs don’t know the difference between steps which are important/easy/hard/intuitive/non-intuitive for human mathematicians, so lots of the proofs they produce are extremely clunky and pedantic in places and dwell for ages over details that are obvious and would usually be skipped over and then will move very fast through things that justify more attention. This unevenness is part of what makes their proofs hard for humans to work through, but also means they are generally poor judges of what would actually constitute a decent simplification.
Proof and program are twins. Formalized theorems can be incompatible for exactly the same reasons that programming APIs can be incompatible.

Uhm three ideas about that (they don't solve the problem on their own, they just show mathematicians care about this issue)

Category theory can be viewed as a framework to make math more modular and compatible. For example topos theory can be used to transport definitions to other "mathematical universes" of sorts

Another point of view is that is working with synthetic mathematics which is a bit like "programming" mathematics with an abstract API. The opposite, analytic mathematics, leak implementation details (for example, the von Neumann construction of natural numbers, which is analytic, leak the implementation detail that 0 is defined as the empty set; but the peano axioms are synthetic and doesn't leak any such details)

There is also the principle that two mathematical objects that are isomorphic (have the same structure) are actually the same thing. For example if you construct the natural numbers two different ways, they are "the same thing" in a sense. This usually is stated informally, but a rigorous formulation of that is the univalent principle

A few unrelated examples:

Some books assume 0 is Natural but other start from 1.

In some books all Rings https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_(mathematics) have a multiplicative identity. Almost all books assume Algebras have an identity, but there may be weird cases.

Some books say in the first page that they will assume all groups are Abelian/Commutative, and not repeat the assumption in each page.

There are like 8 conventions to define the Fourier Transform. All are equivalent, but each one add different constants here and there. Beware to combine formulas from different books.

I guess it's easier for the computer to track the details and remember to translate the names in each book article to a consistent set of definitions.

The second feels like where the "coherent whole" cost actually sits, and I'm curious how much of the 500-source effort was that reconciliation versus line-by-line translation.

Im' not sure he'd say that -- Per Martin-Löf's original work was to develop a computational and predicative foundation for constructive mathematics à la Bishop.

Lean's type theory kinda gives up on that idea: Mathlib gleefully postulates impredicative propositions with the axiom of choice, quotient types, etc. All in all, I'd say that Lean is much closer in spirit to De Bruijn's AUTOMATH project (which pre-dates Martin-Löf!), whose goal was to formalise classical math textbooks using dependent types.

I am saying that Martin-Löf would see his work in Lean, not mathlib. Mathlib is a library. In Lean you can "contain" classic reasoning to certain parts of the code base, and that is also true in the original MLTT: you can postulate classical axioms as functions in scope.
Even without Mathlib, Lean's type theory is impredicative. Martin-Löf does not consider impredicativity to be constructive.

Well, the point of the _computer_ formalization is that it's checkable.

An error in the formalization would be a bug in lean. Which, as we know, certainly seems plausible (I've mused on if these giant proofs are incentivizing LLMs to find lean bugs to exploit), but at least it's a smaller surface area.
An error in the formalization could also be that you formally prove something different from what you think you proved.

All that needs to be checked to avoid that is the statement of the main theorem. Any divergence further inside means you proved the main theorem differently than you thought you did -- but you still proved it.

This assumes the Lean kernel itself isn't bugged, but getting it correct is a matter that affects all uses, not just this one, so the cost of making it correct is spread over all those uses.

In general checking that the definitions are correct isn't that hard and assuming at least one of the lean kernels you verify with is correct (which tbf is an assumption, the implementations are based on each other so could have a common bug) that's all you need to verify.

In this case the statement is unusually complicated but still much much easier to verify than the proof itself.

So, the specification of the theorem we are fairly solid on, formalising what a group is, and a simple group, have been done a long time and we are confident in the correctness of.

Assuming you do trust those, then assuming the formalisation passes lean (and lean has no bugs!), then the whole idea is you've got a proof of the theorem.

The papers describing lean and it's core operations are deliberately small. The kernel of a theorem prover is meant to be such that a human can check it for correctness. The kernel does not include things like type inference or execution. It literally checks the proof and that's all and everything needs to match exactly. It's fairly trivial to write such a thing.

Humans have to establish trust in this.

After that, the rest of the language is written. Yes it is possible the type inference engine is broken but in that case the kernel will reject it
